script: Hello, everyone. This is a message from the Student Center. Every week, students leave many things around campus, like phones, keys, umbrellas, and water bottles. All of these things go to our Lost and Found office. The office is on the first floor of the Student Center, next to the post office. It is open from nine to five, Monday to Friday. If you lost something, please come and look. You will need to show your student card to take an item home. We keep everything for thirty days. After that, we give clothes and bags to a local charity. Thank you, and please check your things before you leave a classroom!

script: Today, I want to tell you about one of the smartest animals in the ocean: the octopus. An octopus has eight arms and no bones, so it can fit through very small holes. In fact, if its beak can get through a hole, the whole octopus can get through. The octopus is also a master of hiding. Its skin has special cells that can change color in less than one second. It can look like a rock, sand, or even a plant. But what really surprises scientists is how well octopuses solve problems. In one experiment, researchers put food inside a glass jar with a lid. The octopus looked at the jar, held it with its arms, and opened the lid. Some octopuses learned to do this faster each time. Here is another interesting fact. Most of an octopus's brain cells are not in its head. They are in its arms. This means each arm can touch, taste, and move a little on its own. So, in a way, an octopus thinks with its whole body. Next time, we'll compare the octopus with its relative, the squid.

script: Good morning. Today we're going to look at plants that live in the desert, especially the cactus. Deserts get very little rain. In some deserts, it rains only a few times a year. So how does a cactus stay alive? First, think about its roots. Many cactus roots do not go deep. Instead, they spread out wide, just under the ground. When it rains, even a little, these roots can quickly catch the water before it dries up. Second, the cactus stores water inside its thick stem. After a big rain, the stem can grow fatter, like a sponge. Then the plant uses this water slowly for many months. Third, look at the spines. A cactus doesn't have normal leaves. Leaves lose a lot of water into the air. Spines lose much less. The spines also protect the cactus from animals that want to drink the water inside. And they give a little shade to the stem. Finally, many cacti open their small air holes only at night, when the air is cool. This also helps them save water. So the cactus is really a water-saving machine.

script: Let's start today with a simple question. Why do we see rainbows? To understand this, we first need to know something about sunlight. Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of many colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. Usually we can't see these colors separately. Now, imagine it has just rained, and there are millions of tiny water drops in the air. When sunlight goes into a water drop, the light bends. Each color bends a little differently. Red bends the least, and violet bends the most. So the colors separate. The light then bounces off the back of the drop and comes out again toward your eyes. That is why you see a band of colors in the sky. Here is a useful tip. You can only see a rainbow when the sun is behind you and the rain is in front of you. That's why rainbows are most common in the early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low. If the sun is high in the sky at noon, the rainbow is below the horizon, so you can't see it. Sometimes you can even see a second, lighter rainbow above the first one.

translation: 오늘은 간단한 질문으로 시작하겠습니다. 우리는 왜 무지개를 볼까요? 이를 이해하려면 먼저 햇빛에 대해 알아야 합니다. 햇빛은 하얗게 보이지만 사실 빨강, 주황, 노랑, 초록, 파랑, 보라 등 많은 색이 섞여 있습니다. 보통은 이 색들을 따로 볼 수 없습니다. 이제 비가 막 그쳐서 공기 중에 아주 작은 물방울이 수백만 개 있다고 상상해 보세요. 햇빛이 물방울에 들어가면 빛이 꺾입니다. 색마다 조금씩 다르게 꺾입니다. 빨강이 가장 적게, 보라가 가장 많이 꺾입니다. 그래서 색이 나뉩니다. 그 빛은 물방울 뒤쪽에서 반사되어 다시 여러분의 눈 쪽으로 나옵니다. 그래서 하늘에 색의 띠가 보이는 것입니다. 유용한 팁이 하나 있습니다. 무지개는 해가 뒤에 있고 비가 앞에 있을 때만 볼 수 있습니다. 그래서 해가 낮게 떠 있는 이른 아침이나 늦은 오후에 무지개가 가장 흔합니다. 정오에 해가 하늘 높이 있으면 무지개가 지평선 아래에 생겨서 볼 수 없습니다. 가끔은 첫 무지개 위에 더 옅은 두 번째 무지개가 보이기도 합니다.

script: Today, let's talk about something you use every day but probably never think about: paper. Before paper, people wrote on many different things. In ancient Egypt, they used papyrus, which was made from a plant that grew by the river. In Europe, people often wrote on animal skins. These materials worked, but they were expensive or heavy. Paper as we know it was first made in China about two thousand years ago. A government worker named Cai Lun is often given credit for it. He mixed tree bark, old cloth, and even fishing nets with water. He beat the mix into a soft paste, spread it thin on a screen, and let it dry. The result was light, cheap, and easy to write on. For hundreds of years, the Chinese kept this method mostly to themselves. Then, in the eighth century, papermaking spread to the Middle East. Cities like Baghdad built paper mills, and books became much more common there. Later, the knowledge moved to Europe. Cheap paper made it possible for more people to read and share ideas. So this simple material changed how knowledge traveled around the world.

questions.explanation: 교수는 파피루스와 동물 가죽이 비싸거나 무거웠다고 말한 뒤, 가볍고 싼 종이를 소개합니다. 종이 이전의 상황과 비교해 종이의 장점을 보여 주려는 것입니다.

translation: 오늘은 여러분이 매일 쓰지만 아마 한 번도 생각해 보지 않았을 종이에 대해 이야기해 봅시다. 종이 이전에 사람들은 여러 가지에 글을 썼습니다. 고대 이집트에서는 강가에서 자라는 식물로 만든 파피루스를 썼습니다. 유럽에서는 흔히 동물 가죽에 글을 썼습니다. 이 재료들은 쓸 만했지만 비싸거나 무거웠습니다. 우리가 아는 종이는 약 2천 년 전 중국에서 처음 만들어졌습니다. 흔히 채륜이라는 관리가 그 공을 인정받습니다. 그는 나무껍질, 낡은 천, 심지어 어망까지 물과 섞었습니다. 그 혼합물을 두드려 부드러운 반죽으로 만들고, 체 위에 얇게 펴서 말렸습니다. 그 결과물은 가볍고 싸고 글을 쓰기 쉬웠습니다. 수백 년 동안 중국인들은 이 방법을 대체로 자기들만 알고 있었습니다. 그러다 8세기에 제지술이 중동으로 퍼졌습니다. 바그다드 같은 도시에 제지 공장이 세워졌고, 그곳에서 책이 훨씬 흔해졌습니다. 나중에 이 지식은 유럽으로 건너갔습니다. 값싼 종이 덕분에 더 많은 사람이 글을 읽고 생각을 나눌 수 있게 되었습니다. 이렇게 이 단순한 재료가 지식이 세계를 오가는 방식을 바꾸었습니다.

script: How many hours did you sleep last night? Many college students sleep only five or six hours. Today, I want to explain why sleep is so important for learning. Scientists used to think that the brain simply rests when we sleep. Now we know that the brain is very busy at night. During sleep, the brain goes through different stages. In deep sleep, the brain replays what you learned during the day. It moves new information into long-term memory, a bit like saving a file on a computer. In another stage, called REM sleep, we have most of our dreams. This stage seems to help us connect ideas and solve problems in new ways. In one study, students learned a list of words in the evening. Half of them slept for eight hours. The other half stayed awake all night. The next day, the students who slept remembered many more words. So staying up all night before an exam is usually a bad plan. You might study more hours, but your brain won't save the information well. Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep. Try it before your next test.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the lecture?
choices: Dreams have no real purpose.
Sleep helps the brain store and use new information.
College students should study at night.
Computers work like human brains.
questions.explanation: 교수는 잠자는 동안 뇌가 낮에 배운 것을 장기 기억으로 옮기고 생각을 연결한다고 설명합니다. 강의의 핵심은 잠이 학습에 중요하다는 것입니다.

questions.q: According to the professor, what happens during deep sleep?
choices: The brain moves new information into long-term memory.
The brain stops working.
We have most of our dreams.
The body grows taller.
questions.explanation: 깊은 잠에서는 뇌가 낮에 배운 것을 다시 재생해 장기 기억으로 옮긴다고 했습니다. 꿈을 가장 많이 꾸는 단계는 렘수면입니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor compare the brain to saving a file on a computer?
choices: To show that computers are smarter than brains
To make it easier to understand how memories are stored
To suggest that students use computers to study
To explain why dreams are strange
questions.explanation: 새 정보가 장기 기억으로 옮겨지는 과정을 컴퓨터 파일 저장에 비유해 쉽게 설명하려는 것입니다.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about studying all night before an exam?
choices: It is the best way to prepare.
It is only a problem for older students.
It may not help because the brain cannot save information well.
It improves REM sleep the next night.
questions.explanation: 교수는 밤을 새우면 공부 시간은 늘어도 뇌가 정보를 잘 저장하지 못한다고 말합니다. 그래서 시험 전날 밤샘은 대개 나쁜 계획이라고 합니다.

translation: 어젯밤에 몇 시간 잤나요? 많은 대학생이 5~6시간밖에 자지 않습니다. 오늘은 잠이 학습에 왜 그렇게 중요한지 설명하겠습니다. 과학자들은 예전에 우리가 잘 때 뇌가 그냥 쉰다고 생각했습니다. 이제 우리는 밤에 뇌가 매우 바쁘다는 것을 압니다. 잠자는 동안 뇌는 여러 단계를 거칩니다. 깊은 잠에서는 뇌가 낮에 배운 것을 다시 재생합니다. 새 정보를 장기 기억으로 옮기는데, 컴퓨터에 파일을 저장하는 것과 비슷합니다. 렘수면이라는 다른 단계에서는 꿈을 가장 많이 꿉니다. 이 단계는 생각을 연결하고 문제를 새로운 방식으로 푸는 데 도움이 되는 것 같습니다. 한 연구에서 학생들이 저녁에 단어 목록을 외웠습니다. 절반은 8시간을 잤습니다. 나머지 절반은 밤새 깨어 있었습니다. 다음 날, 잠을 잔 학생들이 훨씬 많은 단어를 기억했습니다. 그러니 시험 전날 밤을 새우는 것은 대개 나쁜 계획입니다. 공부 시간은 늘지 몰라도 뇌가 정보를 잘 저장하지 못합니다. 대부분의 성인은 7~9시간의 잠이 필요합니다. 다음 시험 전에 한번 해 보세요.

script: Attention, residents of Oakwood Hall. This is Facilities Management. On Thursday morning, we will be replacing an old water pipe under the building. Because of this work, there will be no running water in Oakwood Hall from eight a.m. until about two p.m. That means the showers, sinks, and toilets on all floors will not work during that time. If you need to shower, please do it before eight, or you can use the showers at the recreation center, which will be open early that day just for Oakwood residents. We will also place bottles of drinking water in the main lobby. We're sorry for the trouble. This repair should prevent bigger problems, like leaks, during the winter.

questions.q: Why will the water be turned off?

translation: 오크우드 홀 거주자 여러분께 알립니다. 시설관리팀입니다. 목요일 오전에 건물 아래의 낡은 수도관을 교체할 예정입니다. 이 공사 때문에 오크우드 홀에는 오전 8시부터 오후 2시경까지 물이 나오지 않습니다. 그 시간 동안 모든 층의 샤워실, 세면대, 화장실을 쓸 수 없습니다. 샤워가 필요하면 8시 전에 하거나, 그날 오크우드 거주자만을 위해 일찍 문을 여는 레크리에이션 센터 샤워실을 이용하세요. 중앙 로비에 생수도 비치해 두겠습니다. 불편을 드려 죄송합니다. 이번 수리로 겨울철 누수 같은 더 큰 문제를 막을 수 있을 것입니다.

script: Hi, everyone. This is Jenna from the Academic Success Center. I want to remind you that our peer tutoring program is free for all students. Our tutors are juniors and seniors who earned high grades in the courses they teach. This semester we're offering help in math, chemistry, biology, economics, and, for the first time, computer science. You can book a one-hour session through the student portal. If you'd rather work in a small group, we also have drop-in study tables every evening from six to nine in the library. One more thing: we're hiring new tutors for next semester. If you got an A in a course and you enjoy explaining things, please apply by October fifteenth. Tutors are paid fifteen dollars an hour.

choices: Tutoring is free for the first time.
Tutoring in computer science is offered.

questions.q: Why does the speaker mention October fifteenth?

It is the deadline to apply to become a tutor.

script: Hey, filmmakers! The Campus Film Society is now accepting entries for our spring Short Film Festival. Any current student can submit a film, and you don't need to be a film major. Films must be ten minutes or shorter, and this year's theme is home. You can understand that word in any way you like: a place, a family, a memory, or even a feeling. Please upload your film to our website by March first. A group of faculty and students will choose twelve films to show at the festival in April. The top three films will win cash prizes, and the audience will also vote for a favorite. If you need a camera or editing software, you can borrow them from the media lab for free.

questions.explanation: 화자는 봄 단편 영화제 출품을 받는다고 알리며 조건, 주제, 마감일을 설명합니다. 미디어 랩은 장비를 빌리는 곳으로 덧붙인 정보입니다.

questions.q: What does the speaker say about the theme?
choices: It must be about the speaker's family.
It changes every month.
Only film majors may choose it.
Students can interpret it freely.
questions.explanation: 올해 주제는 '집(home)'이며 장소, 가족, 기억, 감정 등 원하는 방식으로 이해해도 된다고 말합니다.

translation: 영화 만드는 여러분, 안녕하세요! 캠퍼스 영화 동아리가 봄 단편 영화제 출품작을 받고 있습니다. 재학생이라면 누구나 영화를 낼 수 있고, 영화 전공일 필요는 없습니다. 영화는 10분 이하여야 하며, 올해 주제는 '집'입니다. 이 단어는 장소, 가족, 기억, 혹은 감정까지 원하는 대로 해석해도 됩니다. 3월 1일까지 웹사이트에 영화를 올려 주세요. 교수와 학생으로 이루어진 심사단이 4월 영화제에서 상영할 12편을 고릅니다. 상위 세 편은 상금을 받고, 관객도 가장 좋아하는 작품에 투표합니다. 카메라나 편집 프로그램이 필요하면 미디어 랩에서 무료로 빌릴 수 있습니다.

script: If you've ever spent a day at the beach, you've probably noticed that the water comes up the sand and then goes back out again. These are the tides, and today we'll look at what causes them. The main cause is the Moon. The Moon's gravity pulls on everything on Earth, but water can move easily, so the oceans respond the most. The side of the Earth that faces the Moon gets pulled a little toward it, and that creates a bulge of water, a high tide. Now, here's the part that surprises many students. There's also a high tide on the opposite side of the Earth, the side facing away from the Moon. That's because the Moon pulls the solid Earth more strongly than it pulls the water on the far side, so that water is sort of left behind. As the Earth turns, most coastlines pass through both bulges every day. That's why many places have two high tides and two low tides about every twenty-four hours. The Sun matters, too. When the Sun and Moon line up, during a full moon or a new moon, their pulls add together and we get extra large tides, called spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season, by the way.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: How beaches are formed
What causes ocean tides
Why the Moon changes shape
How sailors predict the weather
questions.explanation: 교수는 해변에서 물이 들어왔다 나가는 현상을 예로 들고, 달과 태양의 인력이 조수를 만드는 원리를 설명합니다.

questions.q: According to the professor, why is there a high tide on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon?
choices: The Sun pulls the water on that side.
The Moon pulls the solid Earth more strongly than the far water.
Winds push the water to that side.
The water there is warmer and expands.
questions.explanation: 달이 먼 쪽의 물보다 단단한 지구 자체를 더 세게 당기기 때문에 그쪽 물이 '뒤에 남겨져' 만조가 생긴다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: When do spring tides occur?
choices: Only during the spring season
When there is no wind
When the Moon is farthest from Earth
When the Sun and Moon line up
questions.explanation: 보름달이나 그믐달(삭) 무렵 태양과 달이 일직선이 되면 두 힘이 더해져 큰 조수인 사리(spring tide)가 생긴다고 합니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor say the name has nothing to do with the season?
choices: To introduce a new topic about seasons
To explain that tides are smaller in spring
To correct a likely misunderstanding about the term
To show that the term is no longer used
questions.explanation: spring tide라는 이름 때문에 학생들이 봄철과 관련 있다고 오해할 수 있으므로 미리 바로잡아 주는 말입니다.

translation: 해변에서 하루를 보내 본 적이 있다면 물이 모래 위로 올라왔다가 다시 빠져나가는 것을 보았을 겁니다. 이것이 조수이고, 오늘은 무엇이 조수를 일으키는지 알아보겠습니다. 주된 원인은 달입니다. 달의 중력은 지구의 모든 것을 당기지만, 물은 쉽게 움직이기 때문에 바다가 가장 크게 반응합니다. 달을 향한 지구 쪽은 달 쪽으로 조금 당겨지고, 그래서 물이 불룩해지는 만조가 생깁니다. 이제 많은 학생이 놀라는 부분입니다. 지구의 반대편, 즉 달을 등진 쪽에도 만조가 생깁니다. 달이 먼 쪽의 물보다 단단한 지구를 더 세게 당기기 때문에, 그쪽 물이 말하자면 뒤에 남겨지는 것입니다. 지구가 자전하면서 대부분의 해안은 매일 두 개의 불룩한 부분을 모두 지나갑니다. 그래서 많은 곳에서 약 24시간마다 만조 두 번, 간조 두 번이 있습니다. 태양도 영향을 줍니다. 보름달이나 그믐달(삭) 때처럼 태양과 달이 일직선이 되면 두 힘이 합쳐져 특히 큰 조수가 생기는데, 이를 사리(spring tide)라고 합니다. 참고로 이 이름은 계절 봄과는 아무 관련이 없습니다.

script: Have you ever gone to a store to buy one cheap item and left with a full shopping bag? If so, you may have experienced a strategy called a loss leader. A loss leader is a product that a store sells at a very low price, sometimes even below what the store paid for it. So the store actually loses money on every one it sells. Why would a business do that? Well, the store isn't really trying to make money on that item. It's trying to get you through the door. Supermarkets do this all the time with things like milk or eggs. They advertise a great price, you come in, and while you're there, you also buy bread, snacks, and cleaning supplies, which have normal prices. The profit on those other items is greater than the loss on the milk. Notice also where stores put these products. Milk is often at the very back of a supermarket, so you walk past many other shelves to reach it. Of course, the strategy has risks. Some shoppers, sometimes called cherry pickers, buy only the cheap items and leave. If too many customers do that, the store loses money. So managers need to choose loss leaders carefully, usually products that people buy often and that lead to other purchases.

questions.q: What is a loss leader?
choices: A product sold very cheaply to attract customers
A manager who loses money for a company
A customer who only buys cheap items
A product placed at the front of a store
questions.explanation: loss leader는 가게가 손해를 보더라도 아주 싼 값에 파는 상품으로, 손님을 가게 안으로 끌어들이려는 목적이 있다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention milk being at the back of supermarkets?
choices: To explain how stores make customers pass other products
To show that milk needs to be kept cold
To complain about supermarket design
To show that milk is not a popular product
questions.explanation: 우유를 매장 맨 뒤에 두면 손님이 다른 진열대를 많이 지나가게 되어 다른 상품도 사게 된다는 점을 보여 주려는 예입니다.

questions.q: What problem do cherry pickers cause?
choices: They buy only the cheap items, so the store loses money.
They complain about high prices.
They take too long at the checkout.
They return products after buying them.
questions.explanation: 체리 피커는 싼 상품만 사고 떠나는 손님이어서, 이런 손님이 많으면 가게가 손해를 본다고 합니다.

questions.q: What kind of product would probably make the best loss leader?
choices: An expensive item that people buy once in ten years
A product that is difficult to find in other stores
A product people buy often that leads to other purchases
A product that customers rarely notice
questions.explanation: 교수는 사람들이 자주 사고 다른 구매로 이어지는 상품을 신중하게 고른다고 말합니다. 따라서 자주 사는 생필품이 가장 적합하다고 추론할 수 있습니다.

translation: 싼 물건 하나를 사러 가게에 갔다가 장바구니를 가득 채워 나온 적이 있나요? 그렇다면 '미끼 상품'이라는 전략을 경험했을 수 있습니다. 미끼 상품은 가게가 아주 낮은 가격, 때로는 들여온 가격보다도 낮게 파는 상품입니다. 그래서 가게는 하나 팔 때마다 실제로 손해를 봅니다. 기업이 왜 그럴까요? 가게는 그 상품으로 돈을 벌려는 것이 아닙니다. 여러분을 가게 안으로 들어오게 하려는 것입니다. 슈퍼마켓은 우유나 달걀 같은 것으로 늘 이렇게 합니다. 좋은 가격을 광고하면 여러분이 들어오고, 들어온 김에 정상 가격인 빵, 과자, 세제도 삽니다. 그 다른 상품들의 이익이 우유에서 본 손해보다 큽니다. 가게가 이런 상품을 어디에 두는지도 보세요. 우유는 흔히 슈퍼마켓 맨 뒤에 있어서, 그곳까지 가려면 많은 진열대를 지나가야 합니다. 물론 이 전략에도 위험이 있습니다. 흔히 '체리 피커'라 불리는 일부 손님은 싼 상품만 사고 떠납니다. 그런 손님이 너무 많으면 가게는 손해를 봅니다. 그래서 관리자는 보통 사람들이 자주 사고 다른 구매로 이어지는 상품을 미끼 상품으로 신중하게 골라야 합니다.

script: In the year seventy-nine, the volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted in southern Italy. Within about a day, the Roman town of Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and stone. It was a terrible disaster for the people who lived there. But for archaeologists, it's one of the most valuable sites in the world. Why? Most ancient towns changed slowly over hundreds of years. People tore down old buildings and built new ones on top. Things were lost, moved, or reused. Pompeii is different. Because it was covered so quickly, it's like a photograph of a single day in Roman life. Archaeologists have found bread still in ovens, paintings on walls, and even messages that people wrote on buildings. Some of these messages are election signs, and some are jokes or love notes. They tell us how ordinary people thought and spoke, not just emperors and generals. In the eighteen hundreds, an archaeologist named Giuseppe Fiorelli noticed empty spaces in the hardened ash. He realized they were the shapes of people's bodies. He filled the spaces with plaster, and the result was casts that show people in their last moments. Today, about one third of the town still hasn't been dug up. Archaeologists are leaving some of it for the future, when better tools may allow them to learn even more.

questions.q: Why is Pompeii especially valuable to archaeologists?
choices: It was buried quickly, so it shows a single moment of daily life.
It was the largest city in the Roman Empire.
It was built on top of an older town.
It was where Roman emperors lived.
questions.explanation: 다른 고대 도시는 오랜 세월 바뀌었지만, 폼페이는 순식간에 묻혀 로마인의 하루를 찍은 사진 같다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: What does the professor say about the messages written on buildings?
choices: They show how ordinary people thought and spoke.
They were written only by government officials.
They were added by later visitors.
They describe the volcanic eruption.
questions.explanation: 선거 홍보, 농담, 사랑 고백 같은 낙서가 황제나 장군이 아닌 평범한 사람들의 생각과 말투를 보여 준다고 합니다.

questions.q: What did Giuseppe Fiorelli do?
choices: He filled empty spaces in the ash with plaster.
He predicted the eruption.
He removed all the paintings from the walls.
He found bread in the ovens.
questions.explanation: 피오렐리는 굳은 화산재 속 빈 공간이 사람 몸의 형태라는 것을 깨닫고 석고를 부어 형상을 만들었습니다.

questions.q: Why are archaeologists leaving part of Pompeii unexcavated?
choices: Future tools may help them learn more.
They have lost interest in the site.
The area is too dangerous to dig.
The government does not allow it.
questions.explanation: 교수는 앞으로 더 좋은 도구가 생기면 더 많이 알아낼 수 있도록 일부를 남겨 두고 있다고 말합니다.

translation: 79년에 이탈리아 남부의 베수비오 화산이 분화했습니다. 하루 정도 만에 로마 도시 폼페이는 몇 미터 두께의 화산재와 돌 아래 묻혔습니다. 그곳에 살던 사람들에게는 끔찍한 재앙이었습니다. 하지만 고고학자에게는 세계에서 가장 귀중한 유적 중 하나입니다. 왜일까요? 대부분의 고대 도시는 수백 년에 걸쳐 천천히 바뀌었습니다. 사람들은 옛 건물을 허물고 그 위에 새 건물을 지었습니다. 물건은 사라지거나 옮겨지거나 다시 쓰였습니다. 폼페이는 다릅니다. 아주 빨리 덮였기 때문에 로마인 삶의 하루를 찍은 사진과 같습니다. 고고학자들은 아직 오븐 안에 있는 빵, 벽화, 그리고 사람들이 건물에 써 놓은 글까지 발견했습니다. 이 글 중 일부는 선거 홍보이고, 일부는 농담이나 사랑의 쪽지입니다. 이것들은 황제나 장군만이 아니라 평범한 사람들이 어떻게 생각하고 말했는지 알려 줍니다. 1800년대에 주세페 피오렐리라는 고고학자가 굳은 화산재 속의 빈 공간을 발견했습니다. 그는 그것이 사람 몸의 형태라는 것을 깨달았습니다. 그 공간을 석고로 채웠고, 그 결과 사람들의 마지막 순간을 보여 주는 형상이 만들어졌습니다. 오늘날에도 도시의 약 3분의 1은 아직 발굴되지 않았습니다. 고고학자들은 더 나은 도구로 더 많은 것을 알아낼 수 있을 미래를 위해 일부를 남겨 두고 있습니다.

script: Every fall, billions of birds fly south, sometimes thousands of kilometers, and every spring they come back, often to the very same tree. Today's question is: how do they find their way? It turns out birds use several tools, a bit like a traveler who carries a map, a compass, and a watch. The first tool is the Sun. Birds can tell direction from the Sun's position, and they adjust for the time of day using their internal clock. But many birds migrate at night. So the second tool is the stars. In a famous experiment, researchers put young birds in a planetarium, a building where stars are projected onto a ceiling. When the scientists rotated the star pattern, the birds changed the direction they tried to fly. The third tool is the most mysterious: Earth's magnetic field. Birds seem to sense it, which helps them even on cloudy nights when they can't see the Sun or the stars. Finally, when birds get close to home, they use landmarks such as rivers, mountains, and coastlines. Some may even use smell. Having several tools is important, because if one doesn't work, say, on a cloudy day, the bird can depend on another.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
choices: Why birds fly south in the fall
The methods birds use to navigate during migration
How planetariums are built
Which birds fly the longest distances
questions.explanation: 교수는 철새가 길을 찾는 방법으로 태양, 별, 지구 자기장, 지형지물을 차례로 설명합니다.

questions.q: What happened in the planetarium experiment?
choices: The birds changed direction when the star pattern was rotated.
The birds fell asleep under the stars.
The birds ignored the stars completely.
The birds used smell to find the exit.
questions.explanation: 과학자들이 별 배치를 돌리자 새들이 날아가려는 방향을 바꾸었습니다. 새가 별을 보고 방향을 잡는다는 증거입니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor compare birds to a traveler with a map, a compass, and a watch?
choices: To show that birds use several different tools to find their way
To suggest that people learned navigation from birds
To explain how scientists track birds
To argue that birds are better than people at travel
questions.explanation: 새가 길을 찾을 때 여러 가지 도구를 함께 쓴다는 점을 여행자의 지도·나침반·시계에 빗대어 설명한 것입니다.

questions.q: According to the professor, why is it useful for birds to have several tools?
choices: Birds can fly faster with more tools.
It helps them find food along the way.
Young birds need more tools than adults.
If one tool does not work, they can rely on another.
questions.explanation: 마지막에 교수는 흐린 날처럼 한 가지 도구가 통하지 않을 때 다른 도구에 의지할 수 있어 여러 도구가 중요하다고 말합니다.

translation: 매년 가을 수십억 마리의 새가 때로는 수천 킬로미터를 날아 남쪽으로 가고, 매년 봄에는 흔히 바로 그 나무로 돌아옵니다. 오늘의 질문은 이것입니다. 새들은 어떻게 길을 찾을까요? 알고 보니 새들은 지도, 나침반, 시계를 가진 여행자처럼 여러 도구를 씁니다. 첫 번째 도구는 태양입니다. 새들은 태양의 위치로 방향을 알 수 있고, 체내 시계를 이용해 하루 중 시간에 따라 보정합니다. 하지만 많은 새는 밤에 이동합니다. 그래서 두 번째 도구는 별입니다. 유명한 실험에서 연구자들이 어린 새들을 천장에 별을 비추는 건물인 천체투영관에 넣었습니다. 과학자들이 별 배치를 돌리자 새들이 날아가려는 방향을 바꾸었습니다. 세 번째 도구는 가장 신비로운 지구 자기장입니다. 새들은 자기장을 감지하는 것으로 보이며, 덕분에 태양도 별도 보이지 않는 흐린 밤에도 길을 찾습니다. 마지막으로 집 가까이 오면 강, 산, 해안선 같은 지형지물을 이용합니다. 냄새를 이용하는 새도 있을 수 있습니다. 여러 도구를 가진 것이 중요한 이유는, 이를테면 흐린 날처럼 하나가 통하지 않을 때 다른 것에 의지할 수 있기 때문입니다.

script: Leave an iron nail outside for a few weeks, and it will turn a reddish brown color. We call this rust. Today I want to explain what rust really is, because it's a great example of a chemical reaction you can see in everyday life. Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen. But here's the key point: it needs water, too. Iron in completely dry air rusts very, very slowly. That's why old cars rust much faster in rainy places. Salt makes it even worse, because salt water helps the reaction happen more quickly. In cold regions where people put salt on roads in winter, cars often rust underneath. Now, rust isn't just ugly. It's actually a different substance from iron. It's weaker, and it flakes off, so fresh iron underneath is exposed and the process continues. Over time, a bridge or a ship can lose a lot of its strength. So how do we stop it? One way is to block water and oxygen with paint or oil. Another way is to cover iron with a thin layer of zinc. This is called galvanizing. The zinc reacts first, so it protects the iron, even if the surface gets scratched. Interestingly, some metals like aluminum also react with oxygen, but they form a thin, tight layer that actually protects the metal inside.

questions.q: According to the professor, what does iron need in order to rust quickly?
choices: Oxygen and water
Heat and light
Zinc and salt
Paint and oil
questions.explanation: 녹은 철이 산소와 반응해 생기지만 물도 꼭 필요하다고 강조합니다. 완전히 건조한 공기에서는 아주 천천히 녹슨다고 합니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention salt on roads?
choices: To explain why roads are slippery in winter
To show how zinc is produced
To give an example of something that speeds up rusting
To describe a way to protect cars
questions.explanation: 소금물이 반응을 빠르게 하므로 겨울에 도로에 소금을 뿌리는 지역의 차들이 아래쪽부터 녹슨다는 예를 든 것입니다.

questions.q: Why does rust keep spreading once it starts?
choices: Rust produces its own water.
Rust turns into zinc.
Rust attracts more salt from the air.
Rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron underneath.
questions.explanation: 녹은 약하고 떨어져 나가기 때문에 그 아래의 새 철이 드러나 과정이 계속된다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about aluminum?
choices: Its reaction with oxygen helps protect it.
It rusts faster than iron.
It does not react with oxygen at all.
It must be galvanized with zinc.
questions.explanation: 알루미늄도 산소와 반응하지만 얇고 단단한 층을 만들어 안쪽 금속을 보호한다고 했습니다. 따라서 산화가 오히려 보호 역할을 한다고 추론할 수 있습니다.

translation: 쇠못을 밖에 몇 주 두면 붉은 갈색으로 변합니다. 우리는 이것을 녹이라고 부릅니다. 오늘은 녹이 정말 무엇인지 설명하려고 합니다. 일상에서 볼 수 있는 화학 반응의 좋은 예이기 때문입니다. 녹은 철이 산소와 반응할 때 생깁니다. 하지만 핵심은 물도 필요하다는 것입니다. 완전히 건조한 공기 속의 철은 아주 아주 천천히 녹습니다. 그래서 비가 많이 오는 곳에서 오래된 차가 훨씬 빨리 녹이 습니다. 소금은 상황을 더 나쁘게 합니다. 소금물은 반응을 더 빨리 일어나게 하기 때문입니다. 겨울에 도로에 소금을 뿌리는 추운 지역에서는 차 아래쪽이 녹스는 경우가 많습니다. 녹은 보기 싫기만 한 것이 아닙니다. 사실 철과는 다른 물질입니다. 더 약하고 떨어져 나가기 때문에 그 아래 새 철이 드러나 과정이 계속됩니다. 시간이 지나면 다리나 배가 강도를 크게 잃을 수 있습니다. 그럼 어떻게 막을까요? 한 가지는 페인트나 기름으로 물과 산소를 막는 것입니다. 다른 방법은 철을 얇은 아연 층으로 덮는 것입니다. 이것을 아연 도금이라고 합니다. 아연이 먼저 반응하기 때문에 표면이 긁혀도 철을 보호합니다. 흥미롭게도 알루미늄 같은 금속도 산소와 반응하지만, 얇고 단단한 층을 만들어 오히려 안쪽 금속을 보호합니다.

script: Good morning. This is a message from Counseling and Psychological Services. Over the past year, demand for our services has grown by nearly forty percent, and many of you have told us that waiting for a walk-in appointment was frustrating. So starting October first, we're changing how first visits work. Instead of coming in and waiting, you'll complete a short phone consultation with a counselor, usually within two business days. During that call, the counselor will help decide whether individual counseling, a support group, or a referral to an off-campus provider is the best fit. Walk-in hours will still be available, but only for urgent situations. And remember, if you're in crisis outside office hours, our twenty-four-hour support line is always available. The number is on the back of your student ID card.

questions.q: Why is the counseling center changing its process?
choices: It is moving to a new building.
Demand has grown and waiting for walk-in visits was frustrating.
It has hired fewer counselors this year.
Students asked for more support groups.
questions.explanation: 화자는 서비스 수요가 약 40% 늘었고 학생들이 자유 방문 대기를 불편해했다고 말한 뒤 변경 사항을 소개합니다.

questions.q: What will happen during the phone consultation?
choices: Students will receive their first full counseling session.
A counselor will help choose the most suitable type of support.
Students will be asked to pay a fee.
Students will schedule a walk-in visit.
questions.explanation: 전화 상담에서 상담사가 개인 상담, 지지 집단, 외부 기관 연계 중 무엇이 가장 적합한지 함께 정한다고 안내합니다.

translation: 안녕하세요. 상담·심리 서비스 센터에서 알려 드립니다. 지난 1년간 저희 서비스 수요가 40% 가까이 늘었고, 많은 분이 자유 방문 상담을 기다리는 것이 답답했다고 말씀해 주셨습니다. 그래서 10월 1일부터 첫 방문 방식을 바꿉니다. 직접 와서 기다리는 대신, 보통 영업일 기준 이틀 안에 상담사와 짧은 전화 상담을 하게 됩니다. 그 통화에서 상담사가 개인 상담, 지지 집단, 외부 기관 연계 중 무엇이 가장 잘 맞는지 결정하도록 도와드립니다. 자유 방문 시간은 계속 운영하지만 긴급한 상황에만 이용할 수 있습니다. 그리고 근무 시간 외에 위기 상황이라면 24시간 상담 전화를 언제든지 이용할 수 있다는 것을 기억하세요. 전화번호는 학생증 뒷면에 있습니다.

script: Hello, everyone. This is Parking and Transportation Services with an important change for next year. Beginning in the fall, first-year students living on campus will no longer be eligible for a parking permit. This decision was made because the new science building is being constructed on Lot C, which removes about four hundred spaces. To make up for this, we're expanding the free shuttle to run every ten minutes during the day and adding a late-night route on weekends. First-year students who need a car for a documented medical reason or for off-campus employment can apply for an exception through our website. Students who already hold permits are not affected. Applications for exceptions open on May first, and spaces are limited, so we encourage you to apply early.

questions.q: Why are first-year residents losing access to parking permits?
choices: Too many first-year students had parking accidents.
The university wants to reduce pollution.
Parking fees have become too expensive.
A construction project is removing hundreds of parking spaces.
questions.explanation: 새 과학관이 C 주차장에 지어져 약 400면이 사라지기 때문이라고 설명합니다.

questions.q: Which first-year student could most likely receive an exception?
choices: A student who wants to drive home on weekends
A student who lives close to the shuttle stop
A student who works at a job off campus

script: Take a look at almost any college campus, including ours, and you'll see something interesting on the lawns: narrow strips of worn-out grass where people have walked again and again. Planners call these desire paths. They form when the official sidewalks don't match where people actually want to go. Usually, a desire path is a shortcut, cutting across a corner instead of following a right angle. For a long time, many planners treated desire paths as a problem. They put up fences or signs telling people to keep off the grass. But more and more designers see them as useful information. A desire path is basically free data about how people move. A well-known story, though it may be partly legend, says that some universities waited a year after building new halls before paving any sidewalks. They let students wear their own paths into the grass, then paved exactly those routes. Whether or not that story is completely true, the idea has influenced design. Some cities now use phone location data or video to study pedestrian movement before they finalize a plan. Of course, not every desire path should become a sidewalk. Some cross sensitive areas, like wetlands, or create safety risks near traffic. So the challenge for planners is to tell the difference between a path that reveals a real need and one that should be redirected.

script: Today's puzzle comes from ancient Greece, and it's called the Ship of Theseus. Theseus was a legendary hero, and the people of Athens supposedly kept his ship in the harbor for centuries as a memorial. Over time, the wooden planks rotted, so they were replaced one by one with new planks. Eventually, every single original piece had been replaced. So here's the question: is it still the same ship? Many people's first answer is yes, because the change happened gradually and the ship kept its shape and its purpose. But the seventeenth-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes added a twist. Suppose someone collected all the old planks as they were removed and later rebuilt them into a ship. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real Ship of Theseus? This isn't just a word game. The same question applies to us. Most of the cells in your body are replaced over the years, and your beliefs and memories change, too. So what makes you the same person you were at age five? Some philosophers say it's physical continuity, others say it's psychological continuity, meaning a connected chain of memories and personality. And the puzzle has practical uses. Courts, for example, have to decide whether a company that has changed every employee and owner is still responsible for its old contracts.

script: When researchers test a new drug, they almost always compare it with a placebo, a pill that looks the same but contains no active medicine. Why bother? Because patients who take a placebo often get better anyway. This is called the placebo effect, and it's surprisingly strong, especially for symptoms like pain, nausea, and fatigue. Part of the explanation is expectation. When you believe a treatment will help, your brain can actually release its own pain-reducing chemicals. Brain scans have shown real physical changes in people who respond to placebos. Some details matter, too. In several studies, two placebo pills worked better than one, and injections worked better than pills. Even the color can make a difference. Blue pills tend to be reported as more calming, and red ones as more stimulating. Now, here's the most puzzling finding. In some experiments, researchers told patients openly that they were getting a placebo with no medicine in it. And many of those patients still reported feeling better. Scientists are still debating why. It may be that the ritual of taking a pill and being cared for is itself helpful. One caution, though. Placebos don't shrink tumors or cure infections. They mainly change how we experience symptoms, so they're not a replacement for real treatment.

choices: Placebos are cheaper to produce.

script: If you grew up with dinosaur movies, you probably picture dinosaurs as giant lizards with scaly skin. That image has changed a lot in the last thirty years. In 1996, scientists in northeastern China described a small dinosaur called Sinosauropteryx. The fossil was unusually well preserved because the animal had been buried in fine volcanic ash near a lake. And along its back and tail, there was a fringe of simple, hair-like filaments. These were early feathers. Since then, dozens of feathered dinosaurs have been found in the same region. Some had simple fuzz, while others had complex feathers like modern birds. Now, these dinosaurs couldn't fly, so why did they have feathers? One idea is insulation, keeping their bodies warm, much like the down on a baby chick. Another is display. In 2010, researchers examined tiny structures inside fossil feathers called melanosomes, which hold color pigment. By comparing their shapes with those in living birds, they could estimate the original colors. Sinosauropteryx, it turns out, had a striped tail of orange-brown and white. Bright patterns like that would be useful for attracting mates or recognizing members of the same species. So feathers probably evolved first for warmth or display, and only later were adapted for flight. This is a good example of what biologists call exaptation, a feature that evolves for one purpose and is later used for another.

questions.q: Why was the Sinosauropteryx fossil so well preserved?
choices: It was frozen in ice.
It was found deep in the ocean.
It was trapped in tree sap.
It was buried in fine volcanic ash near a lake.

translation: 공룡 영화를 보며 자랐다면 아마 공룡을 비늘 피부의 거대한 도마뱀으로 떠올릴 겁니다. 그 이미지는 지난 30년 동안 크게 바뀌었습니다. 1996년 중국 북동부의 과학자들이 시노사우롭테릭스라는 작은 공룡을 발표했습니다. 이 동물은 호수 근처의 고운 화산재에 묻혔기 때문에 화석이 유난히 잘 보존되어 있었습니다. 그리고 등과 꼬리를 따라 털 같은 단순한 섬유가 줄지어 있었습니다. 이것이 초기 깃털이었습니다. 그 뒤로 같은 지역에서 깃털 공룡이 수십 종 발견되었습니다. 어떤 것은 단순한 솜털을, 어떤 것은 현생 조류 같은 복잡한 깃털을 가졌습니다. 그런데 이 공룡들은 날지 못했는데 왜 깃털이 있었을까요? 한 가지 생각은 보온, 즉 병아리의 솜털처럼 몸을 따뜻하게 하는 것입니다. 또 하나는 과시입니다. 2010년 연구자들은 화석 깃털 속에서 색소를 담는 멜라노솜이라는 아주 작은 구조를 조사했습니다. 그 모양을 살아 있는 새의 것과 비교해 원래 색을 추정할 수 있었습니다. 알고 보니 시노사우롭테릭스는 주황빛 갈색과 흰색 줄무늬 꼬리를 가졌습니다. 이런 선명한 무늬는 짝을 끌거나 같은 종을 알아보는 데 유용했을 것입니다. 그러니 깃털은 아마 처음에는 보온이나 과시를 위해 진화했고, 나중에야 비행에 맞게 바뀌었을 것입니다. 이것은 생물학자들이 굴절적응이라고 부르는 것의 좋은 예입니다. 한 가지 목적으로 진화한 특징이 나중에 다른 목적으로 쓰이는 것이죠.

script: When we read a novel by Charles Dickens today, we usually hold a thick book with hundreds of pages. But most of Dickens's original readers didn't experience his novels that way. They read them in installments, small parts published every month or every week, over a year or more. This is called serial publication, and it shaped the novels themselves in important ways. First, think about the economics. A complete novel was expensive in the eighteen thirties, but a monthly part cost only a shilling, so many more people could afford to follow the story. Second, serialization affected structure. Each installment needed to keep readers interested until the next one, so Dickens often ended a part with an unanswered question or a moment of danger, much like a television episode today. That's partly why his novels have so many characters and subplots. Third, and this is the fascinating part, readers could respond while the story was still being written. Dickens watched sales figures closely, and if a part sold poorly, he could change direction. When sales of Martin Chuzzlewit were disappointing, he sent the main character to America, partly to renew interest. Letters from readers sometimes influenced the fate of characters, too. So in a sense, these novels were a conversation between the author and his audience, not a finished product handed down from above.

choices: The childhood of Charles Dickens
The cost of books in the twentieth century
Why Dickens moved to America
How publishing novels in parts influenced Dickens's work

translation: 오늘날 찰스 디킨스의 소설을 읽을 때 우리는 보통 수백 쪽짜리 두꺼운 책을 들고 있습니다. 하지만 디킨스의 원래 독자 대부분은 그렇게 소설을 경험하지 않았습니다. 그들은 1년 넘게 매달이나 매주 나오는 짧은 회차로 소설을 읽었습니다. 이것을 연재 출판이라고 하며, 이는 소설 자체를 중요한 방식으로 형성했습니다. 먼저 경제적 측면을 생각해 봅시다. 1830년대에 완결된 소설 한 권은 비쌌지만, 한 달 분량은 1실링밖에 하지 않아 훨씬 많은 사람이 이야기를 따라갈 수 있었습니다. 둘째, 연재는 구조에 영향을 주었습니다. 각 회차는 다음 회까지 독자의 관심을 붙잡아야 했기 때문에 디킨스는 흔히 오늘날의 TV 에피소드처럼 풀리지 않은 질문이나 위험한 순간으로 회차를 끝냈습니다. 그의 소설에 등장인물과 곁가지 줄거리가 많은 이유도 부분적으로는 이것입니다. 셋째, 그리고 이것이 흥미로운 부분인데, 독자들은 이야기가 아직 쓰이는 중에 반응할 수 있었습니다. 디킨스는 판매량을 꼼꼼히 지켜보았고, 어떤 회차가 잘 팔리지 않으면 방향을 바꿀 수 있었습니다. script: Attention, students involved in research. The module takes roughly three hours and covers informed consent, data privacy, and how to handle situations in which participants may be vulnerable. You don't have to finish it in one sitting; your progress is saved automatically. Please note that the review board will not approve any proposal that lists an undergraduate who hasn't completed the training, so delays on your part could hold up an entire lab's project. Certificates remain valid for three years. If you completed equivalent training at another institution, you may submit it for review instead.

script: Think about the last time you found a job, an apartment, or even a good doctor. Who told you about it? In 1973, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a deliberately strange title: The Strength of Weak Ties. He had interviewed people in a Boston suburb who had recently changed jobs, and he asked how they'd heard about the position. You might expect that close friends and family, what he called strong ties, would be the most helpful. But that's not what he found. Most people had learned about their new job from acquaintances, people they saw only occasionally, like a former coworker or someone from college. Why would weaker relationships be more useful? Granovetter's explanation is about information. Your close friends tend to know each other and move in the same circles, so they mostly know what you already know. Acquaintances, on the other hand, connect you to different social groups. They act as bridges, carrying new information across. Now, this doesn't mean strong ties are unimportant. When people are in crisis, strong ties provide emotional support and practical help, and research suggests that people in insecure situations rely on them heavily. And a large study of a professional networking site published in 2022 added a refinement. It found that moderately weak ties were the most valuable for job mobility, not the very weakest ones. So the relationship isn't simply the weaker the better.

questions.q: What did Granovetter find about how people learned of new jobs?
choices: Most heard about jobs from acquaintances.
Most heard about jobs from close family members.
Most found jobs through newspaper ads.
Most were contacted directly by employers.
questions.explanation: 예상과 달리 대부분은 가끔 보는 지인, 즉 약한 연결로부터 새 일자리 소식을 들었다고 합니다.

questions.q: According to Granovetter, why are weak ties useful?
choices: They connect people to different social groups and new information.
They are more trustworthy than close friends.
They require less time to maintain.
They provide stronger emotional support.
questions.explanation: 가까운 친구들은 같은 정보를 공유하지만 지인은 다른 집단과 이어 주는 다리 역할을 해 새로운 정보를 가져온다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention people in crisis?
choices: To argue that weak ties are always more important
To introduce a study about job interviews
To point out that strong ties also have important functions
To explain why Granovetter chose his title
questions.explanation: 위기 상황에서는 가까운 관계가 정서적·실질적 도움을 준다고 말하며 강한 연결도 중요하다는 균형을 잡는 것입니다.

translation: 최근에 일자리나 아파트, 혹은 좋은 의사를 찾았던 때를 떠올려 보세요. 누가 알려 주었나요? 1973년 사회학자 마크 그라노베터는 일부러 이상한 제목의 논문을 냈습니다. '약한 연결의 힘'입니다. 그는 최근 이직한 보스턴 교외 주민들을 인터뷰하며 그 일자리를 어떻게 알게 되었는지 물었습니다. 그가 '강한 연결'이라 부른 가까운 친구와 가족이 가장 도움이 되었을 거라고 예상할지 모릅니다. 하지만 그가 발견한 것은 그게 아니었습니다. 대부분은 예전 동료나 대학 동기처럼 가끔 보는 지인에게서 새 일자리 소식을 들었습니다. 왜 더 약한 관계가 더 유용할까요? 그라노베터의 설명은 정보에 관한 것입니다. 가까운 친구들은 서로 알고 같은 무리 안에서 움직이는 경향이 있어서, 대개 여러분이 이미 아는 것을 압니다. 반면 지인은 여러분을 다른 사회 집단과 이어 줍니다. 그들은 다리 역할을 하며 새로운 정보를 건너 나릅니다. 그렇다고 강한 연결이 중요하지 않다는 뜻은 아닙니다. 사람들이 위기에 처했을 때 강한 연결은 정서적 지지와 실질적 도움을 주며, 연구에 따르면 불안정한 상황의 사람들은 이에 크게 의존합니다. 그리고 2022년에 발표된 한 직업 네트워킹 사이트에 대한 대규모 연구는 한 가지를 보완했습니다. 이직에 가장 가치 있는 것은 가장 약한 연결이 아니라 적당히 약한 연결이었습니다. 그러니 관계는 단순히 약할수록 좋은 것이 아닙니다.

script: Here's something you can observe in your own kitchen. If you sprinkle a few drops of water on a pan that's only moderately hot, say a little above a hundred degrees Celsius, they hiss and boil away within a second or two. But if the pan is much hotter, above roughly two hundred degrees, something counterintuitive happens. The drops form little beads that skate around the surface and can last for a minute or more. This is called the Leidenfrost effect, after the German doctor who described it in 1756. So why would water survive longer on a hotter surface? The key is what happens at the very bottom of the drop. When the pan is extremely hot, the water touching it vaporizes instantly and forms a thin layer of steam. That vapor layer lifts the drop slightly off the metal. And because vapor is a poor conductor of heat, it acts like insulation, slowing the transfer of heat into the drop. Meanwhile, the steam continuously escaping from underneath lets the drop glide with almost no friction. Now, the effect isn't just a kitchen curiosity. It's actually a problem in some industrial settings. When engineers try to cool very hot metal parts or nuclear fuel rods by spraying water on them, the vapor layer can reduce cooling efficiency dramatically. Researchers have been experimenting with textured surfaces that break up the vapor layer so that water makes contact and carries heat away. On the other hand, some scientists hope to exploit the effect to move liquids without pumps.

choices: How to cook safely with hot pans

Why water drops last longer on very hot surfaces

script: Let's turn to a concept that comes up constantly in agricultural policy: monoculture, the practice of growing a single crop variety across a large area. Monoculture has obvious advantages. When every plant is genetically similar, they ripen at the same time, respond to the same fertilizer, and can be harvested with the same machines. That uniformity is a big part of why modern farms are so productive. But uniformity has a hidden cost, and history gives us a painful example. In the eighteen forties, a large share of Ireland's population depended on the potato for most of their calories, and much of the crop came from a very small number of varieties. Potatoes are usually grown from pieces of the parent plant rather than seeds, so the plants were close to genetically identical. When a water mold called Phytophthora arrived, almost nothing in the fields could resist it. Crops collapsed across the country, and roughly a million people died. Of course, the famine also had political and economic causes, which historians emphasize, but the biological vulnerability was real. A more recent case is the banana. Most bananas exported today are a single variety, the Cavendish, which replaced an earlier variety wiped out by a fungal disease in the mid twentieth century. Now a new strain of that fungus is spreading and threatening the Cavendish, too. Plant breeders argue that the solution is to preserve genetic diversity, for example in seed banks, so that resistant traits are available when they're needed.

script: In the early nineteen twenties, a young Soviet filmmaker named Lev Kuleshov ran an experiment that film students still talk about. According to the most common account, he took a close-up shot of a well-known actor with a fairly neutral expression. Then he edited that same shot together with three different images. In one version, the actor's face was followed by a bowl of soup. In another, by a child lying in a coffin. In the third, by an attractive woman on a sofa. When audiences watched these sequences, they reportedly praised the actor's performance. They said he looked hungry when he looked at the soup, grief-stricken at the coffin, and full of desire looking at the woman. But of course, it was the exact same footage of his face every time. This became known as the Kuleshov effect. The idea is that viewers don't interpret a shot in isolation; they derive meaning from the relationship between shots. Editing, in other words, isn't just a technical step for removing mistakes. It's a way of creating meaning. That insight became central to Soviet montage theory, and directors like Sergei Eisenstein built entire films around the collision of images. Now, I should point out that Kuleshov's original film no longer exists, and some details of the story may have been exaggerated over time. But modern researchers have repeated versions of the experiment with careful controls, and they have found a real, if smaller, effect. Context does change how people read facial expressions.

script: Why does the United States have essentially two major political parties, while countries like Germany or the Netherlands have five, six, or more parties in their parliaments? Culture and history play a role, but political scientists point to something more mechanical: the rules of the election itself. In the nineteen fifties, the French political scientist Maurice Duverger proposed that single-member districts with plurality voting tend to produce two-party systems. Plurality voting simply means that whoever gets the most votes in a district wins, even if it's less than half. Duverger identified two forces. The first is mechanical. Smaller parties may win, say, fifteen percent of the vote across the country but come first in almost no districts, so they end up with very few seats. The second force is psychological. Voters who prefer a small party realize their vote probably won't help it win, so they switch to whichever major party they dislike least. This is sometimes called strategic voting. Over time, both forces push small parties out. In contrast, under proportional representation, a party that wins fifteen percent of the vote receives roughly fifteen percent of the seats, so voters have less reason to abandon small parties. Now, Duverger's idea is usually called a law, but it's more of a strong tendency. Canada and the United Kingdom use plurality voting, yet they have significant third parties, often because those parties are concentrated in particular regions, where they can actually win districts.

translation: 왜 미국은 사실상 주요 정당이 둘뿐인데, 독일이나 네덜란드 같은 나라는 의회에 정당이 다섯, 여섯 개 이상일까요? 문화와 역사도 영향을 주지만 정치학자들은 더 기계적인 것, 즉 선거 규칙 자체를 지목합니다. 1950년대 프랑스 정치학자 모리스 뒤베르제는 소선거구 다수대표제가 양당제를 낳는 경향이 있다고 주장했습니다. 다수대표제란 과반이 안 되더라도 선거구에서 가장 많은 표를 얻은 사람이 이기는 방식입니다. 뒤베르제는 두 가지 힘을 찾았습니다. 첫째는 기계적인 힘입니다. 작은 정당은 전국적으로 예컨대 15%를 득표해도 1위를 하는 선거구가 거의 없어 의석을 거의 얻지 못합니다. 둘째는 심리적인 힘입니다. 작은 정당을 지지하는 유권자는 자신의 표가 그 정당의 승리에 도움이 안 될 것임을 깨닫고, 덜 싫은 주요 정당으로 표를 옮깁니다. 이를 흔히 전략적 투표라고 합니다. 시간이 지나면서 두 힘 모두 작은 정당을 밀어냅니다. 반면 비례대표제에서는 15%를 득표한 정당이 대략 15%의 의석을 얻으므로 유권자가 작은 정당을 버릴 이유가 적습니다. 뒤베르제의 생각은 보통 '법칙'이라고 불리지만 강한 경향에 가깝습니다. 캐나다와 영국은 다수대표제를 쓰지만 상당한 제3당이 있는데, 흔히 그 정당들이 특정 지역에 몰려 있어 그곳에서는 실제로 선거구를 이길 수 있기 때문입니다.

script: This is a message from the Dean of Undergraduate Studies regarding revisions to the academic standing policy. Under the current system, a student whose term average falls below a two point zero is placed on probation, and two consecutive terms on probation result in dismissal. Analysis of the past decade suggests this approach disproportionately affected students facing temporary hardships, many of whom went on to graduate after reinstatement. Beginning next fall, the policy will introduce an intermediate status called academic recovery. Students in recovery will develop a written plan with an advisor and may take a reduced course load without losing full-time status for financial aid purposes. Dismissal will be considered only if a student in recovery neither meets the plan's benchmarks nor demonstrates measurable progress. Students currently on probation will be transitioned automatically.

questions.q: What prompted the revision of the policy?
choices: Evidence that the old system unfairly affected students with temporary difficulties
A rise in the number of students on probation
Complaints from financial aid officers
A decline in graduation rates among transfer students
questions.explanation: 지난 10년 분석 결과 기존 제도가 일시적 어려움을 겪는 학생에게 불균형적으로 영향을 주었고, 그중 다수는 복학 후 졸업했다는 점이 개정 이유로 제시됩니다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about students in academic recovery?
choices: They will be dismissed if their average stays below two point zero for one term.
They must leave the university for at least one term.
They can keep financial aid eligibility while taking fewer courses.
They are no longer required to meet with an advisor.

script: Good afternoon. Research Computing would like to alert all faculty, postdocs, and graduate researchers to an upcoming migration. Be aware that the two options are not interchangeable. The cloud platform is approved for data containing personally identifiable or health information, whereas the archive is not, although it offers substantially larger quotas at no charge. Projects governed by a data use agreement with an external partner may carry additional restrictions, so consult the agreement before moving anything. Data left on the legacy servers after the deadline will be retained in read-only form for ninety days and then permanently deleted. Staff can schedule bulk transfers for very large datasets.

It will be deleted immediately.

script: On behalf of the University Libraries, I want to explain a decision that will affect many of you. The publisher's proposal would have raised costs by nearly a third over three years, at a time when the library's budget is flat. Effective January first, we'll instead subscribe individually to roughly two hundred titles that account for the overwhelming majority of campus usage. For articles in titles we no longer carry, interlibrary loan will be expedited, and in most cases you'll receive a PDF within twenty-four hours at no cost. We'd also encourage authors to deposit accepted manuscripts in our open repository, which makes your work freely accessible wherever it's published.

script: This is a reminder from the Graduate School for students submitting theses and dissertations this term. By default, all approved dissertations are deposited in the university repository and become publicly accessible immediately. However, you may request an embargo, which delays public release for one, two, or, in exceptional cases, five years. Common justifications include a pending patent application, an agreement with a book publisher, or the presence of sensitive data relating to vulnerable communities. Embargo requests require your advisor's signature and must be submitted with your final deposit, not afterward. script: The traditional picture of perception runs roughly like this: light hits the retina, signals travel up through a hierarchy of brain areas, and at each stage features are assembled, edges, then shapes, then objects, until you finally recognize, say, a coffee cup. Information flows mainly from the bottom up. Over the past two decades, an alternative framework, usually called predictive processing, has inverted that emphasis. On this view, the brain is constantly generating predictions about what it's about to sense, and those predictions flow downward. What travels upward isn't the raw signal so much as the prediction error, the mismatch between what was expected and what actually arrived. If the prediction is accurate, there's little error to pass along, which is, incidentally, an efficient way to use limited neural resources. One piece of supporting evidence comes from anatomy. In the visual system, there are actually more connections running from higher areas down to lower ones than the reverse, which is hard to explain if perception were purely bottom-up. The framework also offers an elegant account of why you can't tickle yourself. When you move your own hand, your brain predicts the resulting sensation precisely, so the error signal is small and the feeling is muted. Some researchers have even extended the idea to certain features of psychosis, proposing that hallucinations may arise when prior expectations are weighted too heavily relative to incoming evidence. I'd caution, though, that the framework is so flexible that critics worry it can accommodate almost any result, which raises the question of whether it's genuinely testable.

questions.q: According to predictive processing, what mainly travels upward in the brain?
choices: The difference between predicted and actual input
The complete raw sensory signal
Memories of past experiences
Instructions for movement
questions.explanation: 이 이론에 따르면 위로 올라가는 것은 날것의 신호라기보다 예측과 실제 입력의 불일치인 예측 오차라고 설명합니다.

To provide anatomical evidence that is hard to explain with a purely bottom-up model

To explain how the retina detects light

questions.q: How does the framework explain why people cannot tickle themselves?
choices: The skin is less sensitive to one's own touch.
The brain ignores all self-generated movement.

choices: It has been disproven by recent experiments.

translation: 지각에 대한 전통적인 그림은 대략 이렇습니다. 빛이 망막에 닿고, 신호가 뇌 영역의 위계를 따라 올라가며, 각 단계에서 특징이 조립됩니다. 가장자리, 그다음 형태, 그다음 사물로 조립되어 마침내 예컨대 커피 컵을 알아봅니다. 정보는 주로 아래에서 위로 흐릅니다. 지난 20년 동안 보통 '예측 처리'라고 불리는 대안적 틀이 이 강조점을 뒤집었습니다. 이 관점에서 뇌는 곧 감지할 것에 대한 예측을 끊임없이 만들어 내고, 그 예측이 아래로 흐릅니다. 위로 올라가는 것은 날것의 신호라기보다 예측 오차, 즉 기대한 것과 실제로 도착한 것의 불일치입니다. 예측이 정확하면 전달할 오차가 거의 없는데, 덧붙이자면 이는 제한된 신경 자원을 쓰는 효율적인 방법입니다. 이를 뒷받침하는 증거 하나는 해부학에서 나옵니다. 시각 체계에서는 상위 영역에서 하위 영역으로 내려가는 연결이 반대 방향보다 실제로 더 많은데, 지각이 순전히 상향식이라면 설명하기 어렵습니다. 이 틀은 왜 스스로를 간지럽힐 수 없는지에 대해서도 깔끔한 설명을 제공합니다. 자기 손을 움직이면 뇌가 그 결과 감각을 정확히 예측하므로 오차 신호가 작고 느낌이 약해집니다. 일부 연구자는 이 생각을 정신증의 특징으로까지 확장해, 들어오는 증거에 비해 사전 기대에 너무 큰 비중이 실릴 때 환각이 생길 수 있다고 제안했습니다. 다만 이 틀이 너무 유연해서 거의 어떤 결과도 수용할 수 있다고 비판자들이 우려한다는 점은 경고해 두겠습니다. 이는 이 이론이 정말 검증 가능한지에 대한 질문을 던집니다.

script: Last week we discussed Karl Popper's proposal that what distinguishes science from non-science is falsifiability. A scientific theory, for Popper, must make predictions that could in principle turn out to be wrong, and scientists should actively try to refute their own theories. It's a bracing, almost heroic picture. In 1962, Thomas Kuhn published The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, and he argued that this picture doesn't match how science has actually worked. Kuhn observed that most scientists, most of the time, are engaged in what he called normal science. They work within a paradigm, a shared framework of theories, methods, and exemplary problems, and they solve puzzles that the paradigm defines. Crucially, when an experiment produces an anomalous result, they usually don't abandon the paradigm. They assume the experiment was flawed, or that some auxiliary assumption needs adjusting. From a Popperian standpoint, that looks like a failure of nerve. But Kuhn suggested it's actually productive: if scientists dropped theories at the first sign of trouble, they'd never develop any theory deeply enough to discover its real limits. Only when anomalies accumulate and resist resolution does a field enter crisis, and then a revolution may replace the old paradigm with a new one, as when Copernican astronomy displaced the Ptolemaic system. Kuhn's most controversial claim was that successive paradigms can be incommensurable, that there's no neutral standard for comparing them. Critics took this to imply that scientific change is irrational, a reading Kuhn himself spent years disputing.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the lecture?
choices: To present Kuhn's account of science as a challenge to Popper's
To defend Popper's view against all criticism
To explain the details of Copernican astronomy
To argue that science is irrational
questions.explanation: 지난 시간의 포퍼 반증주의를 상기한 뒤, 실제 과학이 그렇게 작동하지 않았다는 쿤의 정상 과학·패러다임 설명을 소개합니다.

They publish a new paradigm.

questions.explanation: 정상 과학의 과학자들은 이상 결과가 나와도 패러다임을 버리지 않고 실험이 잘못되었거나 보조 가정을 조정해야 한다고 본다고 설명합니다.

questions.q: Why did Kuhn think that sticking with a paradigm could be productive?
choices: It allows a theory to be developed deeply enough to reveal its real limits.
It saves money on research.
It prevents scientific revolutions from ever happening.
It makes theories easier to falsify.
questions.explanation: 문제가 처음 보일 때마다 이론을 버리면 그 이론의 진짜 한계를 발견할 만큼 깊이 발전시킬 수 없다는 것이 쿤의 논리입니다.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the claim that Kuhn viewed science as irrational?
choices: It accurately reflects Kuhn's own position.
It is an interpretation Kuhn himself rejected.
It was first proposed by Popper.
It is supported by the Copernican example.
questions.explanation: 비판자들이 공약불가능성을 과학 변화가 비합리적이라는 뜻으로 읽었지만, 쿤 자신은 수년간 그 해석에 반박했다고 말합니다.

translation: 지난주에 우리는 과학과 비과학을 구분하는 것이 반증 가능성이라는 칼 포퍼의 제안을 다뤘습니다. 포퍼에게 과학 이론은 원칙적으로 틀린 것으로 드러날 수 있는 예측을 해야 하며, 과학자는 자신의 이론을 적극적으로 반박하려 해야 합니다. 상쾌하고 거의 영웅적인 그림입니다. 1962년 토머스 쿤은 '과학혁명의 구조'를 출간해 이 그림이 과학이 실제로 작동해 온 방식과 맞지 않는다고 주장했습니다. 쿤은 대부분의 과학자가 대부분의 시간 동안 그가 '정상 과학'이라 부른 일을 한다고 보았습니다. 그들은 이론, 방법, 모범 문제의 공유된 틀인 패러다임 안에서 일하며, 패러다임이 정의한 퍼즐을 풉니다. 중요한 것은, 실험이 이상한 결과를 내도 보통 패러다임을 버리지 않는다는 점입니다. 실험에 결함이 있었거나 어떤 보조 가정을 조정해야 한다고 여깁니다. 포퍼의 관점에서 이는 용기의 부족처럼 보입니다. 하지만 쿤은 이것이 사실 생산적이라고 했습니다. 과학자들이 문제의 첫 징후에 이론을 버린다면 어떤 이론도 그 진짜 한계를 발견할 만큼 깊이 발전시키지 못할 것이기 때문입니다. 이상 현상이 쌓이고 해결되지 않을 때에야 분야가 위기에 들어서고, 그때 혁명이 옛 패러다임을 새것으로 대체할 수 있습니다. 코페르니쿠스 천문학이 프톨레마이오스 체계를 밀어낸 것처럼요. 쿤의 가장 논쟁적인 주장은 연속된 패러다임들이 공약불가능할 수 있다는 것, 즉 그것들을 비교할 중립적 기준이 없다는 것이었습니다. 비판자들은 이를 과학의 변화가 비합리적이라는 뜻으로 받아들였고, 쿤 자신은 수년간 그 해석에 반박했습니다.

script: In 1995 and 1996, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park after an absence of about seventy years. What followed has become one of the most widely cited examples of a trophic cascade, in which effects at the top of a food web ripple down through multiple levels. The popular version goes like this. Wolves reduced elk numbers and, just as importantly, changed elk behavior. Elk began avoiding open river valleys where they were vulnerable. Freed from heavy browsing, willows and aspens along the streams recovered. Beavers returned, building dams that altered water flow, and the restored vegetation stabilized riverbanks. You may have seen a viral video claiming that wolves literally changed the course of the rivers. Now, I want to complicate this story, not to dismiss it, but because the debate is instructive. First, the behavioral mechanism, often called the ecology of fear, has been hard to confirm. Studies tracking elk with GPS collars found that elk didn't consistently avoid areas of high wolf risk in the way the theory predicted. Second, other factors changed over the same period. Human hunting of elk outside the park increased, grizzly bears and cougars recovered, and a prolonged drought affected plant growth. Third, in some areas willows haven't rebounded at all, possibly because decades without beavers lowered the water table, leaving the system stuck in an alternative state. So most ecologists today would say wolves contributed to the changes, but the cascade was weaker, patchier, and more multicausal than the tidy narrative suggests.

questions.q: What is a trophic cascade, according to the lecture?
choices: The movement of animals from one park to another
Effects at the top of a food web spreading down through several levels
The process by which rivers change course
A decline in plant species caused by drought
questions.explanation: 영양 단계 연쇄는 먹이 그물 꼭대기의 영향이 여러 단계로 아래까지 파급되는 현상이라고 정의합니다.

choices: Wolves had no effect on the ecosystem.
Wolves contributed, but the effects were more limited and complex than often claimed.

translation: 1995년과 1996년, 약 70년 만에 옐로스톤 국립공원에 늑대를 다시 들여왔습니다. 그 뒤에 일어난 일은 먹이 그물 꼭대기의 영향이 여러 단계로 아래까지 파급되는 '영양 단계 연쇄'의 가장 널리 인용되는 사례가 되었습니다. 대중적인 버전은 이렇습니다. 늑대가 엘크 수를 줄였고, 그만큼 중요하게 엘크의 행동도 바꾸었습니다. 엘크는 공격받기 쉬운 탁 트인 강 계곡을 피하기 시작했습니다. 심하게 뜯어먹히던 데서 벗어나 개울가의 버드나무와 사시나무가 회복되었습니다. 비버가 돌아와 물 흐름을 바꾸는 댐을 지었고, 회복된 식생이 강둑을 안정시켰습니다. 늑대가 말 그대로 강의 흐름을 바꾸었다는 유행 영상을 본 적이 있을 겁니다. 이제 저는 이 이야기를 복잡하게 만들고 싶습니다. 무시하려는 것이 아니라 이 논쟁에서 배울 점이 있기 때문입니다. 첫째, 흔히 '공포의 생태학'이라 불리는 행동 메커니즘은 확인하기 어려웠습니다. GPS 목걸이로 엘크를 추적한 연구들은 엘크가 이론이 예측한 방식으로 늑대 위험이 높은 지역을 일관되게 피하지는 않았음을 발견했습니다. 둘째, 같은 기간에 다른 요인도 바뀌었습니다. 공원 밖에서 사람의 엘크 사냥이 늘었고, 회색곰과 퓨마가 회복되었으며, 오랜 가뭄이 식물 생장에 영향을 주었습니다. 셋째, 일부 지역에서는 버드나무가 전혀 회복되지 않았는데, 아마도 수십 년간 비버가 없어 지하수면이 낮아지면서 생태계가 다른 상태에 갇혔기 때문일 것입니다. 그래서 오늘날 대부분의 생태학자는 늑대가 변화에 기여했지만, 연쇄는 깔끔한 이야기가 말하는 것보다 더 약하고, 고르지 않으며, 원인이 여럿이었다고 말할 것입니다.

script: Historians of climate face an obvious problem: thermometers have been used systematically for only about three centuries, and reliable global records go back even less. So how do we reconstruct temperatures from, say, the thirteenth century? The answer is proxies, natural or human records that respond to climate in measurable ways. Tree rings are perhaps the best known. In regions where growth is limited by temperature, wider rings generally indicate warmer growing seasons, and because rings can be dated to the exact year, they offer remarkable precision. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica provide a much longer reach, hundreds of thousands of years, through the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the ice, which varies with temperature at the time snow fell. But I want to draw your attention to a less familiar category: documentary proxies. In Japan, for instance, records of the dates when cherry trees reached full bloom in Kyoto have been kept, with gaps, for over a thousand years, largely because the blossoms were tied to court festivals. Since bloom timing depends on spring temperatures, these records serve as a thermometer of sorts. Similarly, European vineyard records of grape harvest dates have been used to reconstruct summer temperatures. The difficulty is that documentary sources carry human biases. A harvest might be delayed by war, labor shortages, or changing tastes in wine rather than by weather. So researchers calibrate each proxy against the period where instrumental data overlap, and they gain confidence mainly when independent proxies, say tree rings and harvest dates, point in the same direction.

choices: How thermometers were invented
Methods for reconstructing past climates without instruments
The history of Japanese court festivals
Why ice melts faster in Greenland
questions.explanation: 교수는 온도계 기록이 없는 시대의 기후를 나이테, 빙하 코어, 문헌 기록 같은 대리 지표로 복원하는 방법을 설명합니다.

questions.q: According to the professor, what is a particular advantage of tree rings?
choices: They can be dated to the exact year.
They cover hundreds of thousands of years.
They are found in every region of the world.
They are not affected by temperature.
questions.explanation: 나이테는 정확한 연도까지 연대를 매길 수 있어 놀라운 정밀성을 제공한다고 합니다. 수십만 년의 범위는 빙하 코어의 장점입니다.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention war and labor shortages?
choices: To show how human factors can distort documentary records
To explain why vineyards were abandoned
To describe the economic history of Europe
To argue that harvest records are useless
questions.explanation: 수확이 날씨가 아니라 전쟁, 노동력 부족, 취향 변화로 늦어질 수 있다는 예로, 문헌 기록에 인간적 편향이 섞인다는 점을 보여 줍니다.

questions.q: According to the professor, when do researchers become most confident in their reconstructions?
choices: When a single proxy shows a dramatic change
When documentary records are complete without gaps
When independent proxies agree with each other
When ice cores contradict tree rings
questions.explanation: 연구자들은 나이테와 수확 날짜처럼 서로 독립적인 대리 지표가 같은 방향을 가리킬 때 주로 확신을 얻는다고 말합니다.

translation: 기후 역사학자들은 분명한 문제에 직면합니다. 온도계는 약 3세기 동안만 체계적으로 쓰였고, 믿을 만한 전 지구 기록은 그보다도 짧습니다. 그럼 예컨대 13세기의 기온은 어떻게 복원할까요? 답은 '대리 지표', 즉 기후에 측정 가능한 방식으로 반응하는 자연 또는 인간의 기록입니다. 아마 가장 잘 알려진 것은 나이테일 것입니다. 생장이 기온에 의해 제한되는 지역에서는 대체로 나이테가 넓을수록 생장기가 따뜻했다는 뜻이고, 나이테는 정확한 연도까지 연대를 매길 수 있어 놀라운 정밀성을 줍니다. 그린란드와 남극의 빙하 코어는 얼음 속 산소 동위원소 비율을 통해 훨씬 긴 기간, 수십만 년까지 거슬러 올라갑니다. 이 비율은 눈이 내릴 당시의 기온에 따라 달라집니다. 하지만 저는 덜 익숙한 범주인 문헌 대리 지표에 주목해 보려 합니다. 예를 들어 일본에서는 교토의 벚꽃이 만개한 날짜 기록이 군데군데 빠지긴 했지만 천 년 넘게 남아 있는데, 벚꽃이 궁중 축제와 연결되어 있었기 때문입니다. 개화 시기는 봄 기온에 달려 있으므로 이 기록은 일종의 온도계 역할을 합니다. 마찬가지로 유럽 포도원의 포도 수확 날짜 기록은 여름 기온을 복원하는 데 쓰여 왔습니다. 어려운 점은 문헌 자료에 인간의 편향이 담긴다는 것입니다. 수확은 날씨가 아니라 전쟁, 노동력 부족, 포도주 취향의 변화 때문에 늦어질 수도 있습니다. 그래서 연구자들은 각 대리 지표를 계측 자료와 겹치는 기간에 맞춰 보정하며, 주로 나이테와 수확 날짜처럼 서로 독립적인 대리 지표가 같은 방향을 가리킬 때 확신을 얻습니다.
